tagline: A gravel turnpike connects a rebuilt stagecoach inn with Confederate mountain earthworks.
intro: Camp Allegheny Backway follows the original Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike alignment between Bartow and the top of Allegheny Mountain, with gravel under its winding course. The Federal Highway Administration describes dense forest, abandoned homesteads, rolling meadows and views of distant valleys and high ridges along the backway. It gives the length as 10.58 miles and allows 30–45 minutes for the drive.

Turnpike construction began in 1838, and by 1845 the road extended from Staunton to Weston. Andrew Yeager began managing Traveller’s Repose that year; it became a post office when the mail route arrived in 1847. During the Civil War, Confederate troops occupied the mountain pass to defend the turnpike’s approach to the Shenandoah Valley. The inn was caught in crossfire at Camp Bartow in October 1861 and burned later that winter. The house beside the road is the replacement, rebuilt on the earlier foundations in 1869.

Begin at Bartow, where Traveller’s Repose is now a private house at the lower intersection. Camp Bartow’s earthworks are most visible on the hill between the backway and the main highway. Follow the old alignment uphill through the forest and meadows to Camp Allegheny at the summit, with fortifications on the facing knoll.

moments.title: Traveller's Repose
moments.text: The private house at the lower intersection dates to 1869, after the wartime inn was burned. Andrew Yeager had managed the inn from 1845, serving travelers on the Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike. It was the first stagecoach stop west of Allegheny Mountain. After the fire, his son Peter Dilly Yeager rebuilt on the earlier foundations. The replacement lodge had 22 rooms and a barn with space for 28 horses. The house was expanded again in 1912 and 1928. The present building is a two-story wood-frame farmhouse, a later structure occupying the site of the stagecoach inn.

moments.title: Camp Bartow
moments.text: Camp Bartow’s trenches surround artillery emplacements, with additional gun positions and camp sites included in the historic district. Confederate troops established the camp in September 1861. Union forces attacked on October 3 in the Battle of Greenbrier River. After hours of fighting, Union commander Joseph Reynolds ordered his troops back to Cheat Mountain; the battle was inconclusive. The district also contains a surviving section of the Staunton and Parkersburg Turnpike, constructed between 1838 and 1846. From the backway, the earthworks are most visible on the hill between this road and the main highway.

moments.title: Camp Allegheny
moments.text: Orders to withdraw had reached the Confederates a few days before Union troops attacked on December 13, 1861. After the Union assault failed, Confederate commanders reinforced the mountain camp for the rest of the winter. The winter brought suffering and disease. Losses and the difficulty of supplying the post contributed to its abandonment in April 1862. The historic district includes the hut and campground site, a cemetery, a church site and the Yeager farmstead site, as well as the earthworks. Earthworks, gun positions and fallen chimney remains are visible at the encampment.
moments.notice: Earthworks, gun positions and chimney falls remain visible.

practical: Camp Allegheny: The backway is gravel. Snow may close the road to Camp Allegheny in winter. National Forest fees may apply. (checked 2026-10-11)
